items.reason: Softened period language: source 'their uncivilized laughter' became 'their wild laughter' (Lead decision 1 / hard rule 4). Also 'yet steadfastly shot her red hell' lost 'steadfastly' ('and still kept driving').
items.new: With the hatch lifted off the top of the works, there was now a wide hearth in front of them. On it stood the Tartarean shapes of the pagan harpooners, who are always the stokers on a whale-ship. With huge pronged poles they tossed hissing masses of blubber into the scalding pots or stirred up the fires underneath, until the flames shot out of the doors like curling snakes and snapped at their feet. The smoke rolled away in sullen heaps. Every time the ship pitched, the boiling oil pitched with her, as if it longed to leap into their faces. Across from the mouth of the works, on the far side of the wide wooden hearth, was the windlass, which served as a sea-going sofa. The watch lounged there when they had nothing else to do, staring into the red heat of the fire until their eyes felt scorched in their heads. Their tawny faces, now thick with grime from smoke and sweat, their matted beards, and by contrast the barbaric brilliance of their teeth were all strangely lit up by the flickering blaze of the works. As they told each other their unholy adventures, tales of terror in words of mirth; as their uncivilized laughter forked up out of them like the flames from the furnace; as the harpooners gestured wildly back and forth in front of them with their huge pronged forks and dippers; as the wind howled on, and the sea leaped, and the ship groaned and dove, and yet steadily drove her red hell farther and farther into the blackness of the sea and the night, and scornfully champed the white bone in her mouth, and spat viciously all around her; then the rushing Pequod, loaded with savages and freighted with fire, burning a corpse and plunging into that blackness of darkness, seemed the physical counterpart of her monomaniac commander's soul.

items.reason: 'By a tunnel inserted at the rear': Melville's 'tunnel' is the period word for a funnel (water is poured in to replenish the reservoir); 'pipe' blurs the device.
items.new: Take the fire-board off the front of the try-works and you expose the bare masonry on that side, pierced by the two iron mouths of the furnaces, directly below the pots. These mouths have heavy iron doors. A shallow tank running under the whole enclosed base of the works keeps the fierce heat of the fire from passing into the deck. A funnel fitted at the back keeps this tank topped up with water as fast as it evaporates. There are no outside chimneys; the flues open straight out of the back wall. And here let us go back for a moment.

items.reason: 'lest Truth shake me falsely' is ambiguous; 'shakes me into falsehood' resolves it to one reading. Render as literally as reads naturally (hard rule 5).
items.new: "No fairy fingers can have pressed this gold; devil's claws must have left their marks on it since yesterday," Starbuck murmured to himself, leaning against the bulwarks. "The old man seems to be reading Belshazzar's terrible writing on the wall. I have never looked at the coin closely. He has gone below; let me read it. A dark valley between three mighty peaks that dwell in heaven and almost seem the Trinity, in some faint earthly symbol. So in this valley of Death God surrounds us, and above all our gloom the sun of Righteousness still shines as a beacon and a hope. If we look down, the dark valley shows us her moldy soil; but if we look up, the bright sun meets our eyes halfway to cheer us. Yet, oh, the great sun does not stay put; and if at midnight we would gladly snatch some sweet comfort from him, we look for him in vain! This coin speaks wisely, gently, truly, but still sadly to me. I will leave it, for fear Truth may shake me falsely."

items.reason: 'very gravely and mathematically bowing' - the comic 'mathematically' is flattened to 'precisely'.
items.new: "Well, then," Bunger broke in, "give him your left arm as bait to get back the right. Do you know, gentlemen" — bowing very gravely and with mathematical precision to each captain in turn — "do you know, gentlemen, that Divine Providence has built the whale's digestive organs so mysteriously that he cannot possibly digest even a man's arm completely? And he knows it, too. So what you take for the White Whale's malice is only his clumsiness. He never intends to swallow a single limb; he only means to scare you with feints. But sometimes he is like the old juggler, once a patient of mine in Ceylon, who used to pretend to swallow jackknives, and one day actually let one slip down inside him for real. There it stayed for a year or more, until I gave him an emetic and he threw it up in little tacks, you see. There was no possible way for him to digest that jackknife and fully absorb it into his general bodily system. Yes, Captain Boomer, if you are quick enough about it, and are willing to pawn one arm for the privilege of giving the other a decent burial, why, in that case the arm is yours. Just let the whale have another go at you soon, that's all."

items.reason: 'Flip? ... we flipped it at the rate of ten gallons the hour' - the flip/flipped pun is lost in 'we put it away'.
items.new: The ship named for him deserved the honor; she was very fast and a noble vessel in every way. I went aboard her once at midnight somewhere off the coast of Patagonia and drank good flip down in the forecastle. It was a fine gam we had, and they were all good sports — every soul on board. May they have a short life and a jolly death. And that fine gam I had — long, long after old Ahab set his ivory heel on her planks — brings back to me the noble, solid, Saxon hospitality of that ship. May my parson forget me and the devil remember me if I ever lose sight of it. Flip? Did I say we had flip? Yes, and we flipped it down at ten gallons an hour. And when the squall hit (it's squally down there off Patagonia) and all hands, visitors included, were called to reef topsails, we were so top-heavy that we had to hoist each other aloft in bowlines. Not knowing what we were doing, we furled the tails of our jackets into the sails, so that we hung there, reefed tight in the howling gale, a warning to all drunken sailors. Still, the masts didn't go overboard, and eventually we scrambled down, so sober that we had to pass the flip around again — though the savage salt spray bursting down the forecastle hatch watered it down and pickled it rather too much for my taste.

items.reason: 'The wondrous old man sat' - the source never says Ahab is seated; it says only that his leg was braced against the table leg.
items.new: By now the Pequod was approaching Formosa and the Bashee Isles from the south and west; between them runs one of the tropical passages out of the China seas into the Pacific. So Starbuck found Ahab with a general chart of the eastern archipelagoes spread out in front of him, along with a separate one showing the long eastern coasts of the Japanese islands of Nippon, Matsumae and Shikoku. The wondrous old man, with his back to the gangway door, his snow-white new ivory leg braced against the screwed-down leg of his table and a long jackknife like a pruning-hook in his hand, was frowning and tracing out his old courses again.

items.reason: 'I'm all aleak myself' became 'I'm leaking all over myself', which reads as an unintended bodily joke and loses the ship metaphor that the next sentences extend.
items.new: "And I wasn't speaking or thinking of that at all. Get out! Let it leak! I'm all leaks myself. Yes! Leaks within leaks! Not only full of leaky casks, but those leaky casks are in a leaky ship; and that's a far worse fix than the Pequod's, man. Yet I don't stop to plug my leak, for who can find it down in the deep-loaded hull? And even if it were found, how could anyone hope to plug it in this life's howling gale? Starbuck! I won't have the Burtons hoisted."

items.reason: Source: 'As ... he hammered ..., the Parsee passed silently' - simultaneous. 'Then the Parsee passed by' makes it a subsequent event.
items.new: When that was done, Perth was about to start welding the twelve into one, but Ahab stopped him and said he would weld his own iron. So Ahab hammered away on the anvil with steady, gasping grunts, while Perth handed him the glowing rods one after another and the hard-driven forge sent up its fierce, straight flame. Meanwhile the Parsee passed by without a word and bent his head toward the fire, as though calling down some curse or some blessing on the work. But when Ahab looked up, he slipped away to one side.
